interactions.summary: A student reads Dante's lines about doing worse by keeping faith and about the same stupidity appearing in the Greek example. Jiang immediately highlights the paradox in that phrasing before turning to the Agamemnon and Iphigenia story.
Jiang retells the Trojan War background and frames Agamemnon as the second stupid vow-keeper: he kills Iphigenia to satisfy Artemis and keep the Greek campaign moving.

A student recalls that Clytemnestra took revenge on Agamemnon. Jiang agrees and uses that outcome to argue that Agamemnon should have foreseen the consequence, which is why keeping this vow was stupid rather than noble.

claims.claim: A student reads Dante's line that Jephthah should have admitted he did wrong rather than do something worse by keeping faith.
Jiang says the paradox of the sentence is that keeping faith can itself become the worse act.
The next lines extend the same stupidity from Jephthah to Agamemnon and Iphigenia.
Jiang says Dante is naming two really stupid people: Jephthah and Agamemnon.
Jiang retells the Greek oath around Helen as the reason the Greeks feel bound before the gods to wage total war against Troy once Paris steals her.
Jiang says Agamemnon kills Iphigenia because a prophet tells him Artemis will only restore the wind if he sacrifices his daughter.
Jiang judges Agamemnon's action as stupid even before the revenge because he subordinates his daughter to the logic of the vow and the campaign.
A student answers that Iphigenia's mother Clytemnestra took revenge on Agamemnon.
Jiang says Agamemnon should have been able to predict Clytemnestra's vengeance, which is why the sacrifice is not tragic necessity but foolishness.
Jiang summarizes the moral by saying that even when vows to the gods matter, people still have to use their brains.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang pauses on Dante's shocking formula that someone can do something worse precisely by keeping faith.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is the packet's central paradox and governs both the Jephthah and Agamemnon cases.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang strips the piety away and says the real moral is simple: use your brains, people.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This condenses his reading of vows into an anti-stupidity ethic rather than ritual obedience.

chronology_notes.note: On 2026-06-18 Jiang generalizes the Jephthah paradox into a broader rule: keeping faith can become stupidity when it ignores predictable human consequences, and Agamemnon is his second major example.
